title: AI mapping of sustainability disclosures to reporting standards, with gap list
problem: Sustainability information is spread across many report sections and documents, and before testing the team must find each disclosure, map it to requirements and spot missing baselines, targets or methods.
approach: Language-model tools locate relevant passages, classify them against ESRS-type categories and produce a preliminary gap list, not a compliance conclusion.
Analyst commentary says Deloitte has an AI-powered Omnia ESG tool automating disclosure roadmaps and tracking regulatory requirements.
No time, accuracy or coverage result is published; the analyst describes what the tool does, not how well (vendor-published).
The practitioner confirms each AI-identified disclosure is complete and supported by evidence; the engagement leader approves the tool for the engagement.

title: AI text screening of draft sustainability reports for greenwashing-type claims
problem: Spotting vague, promotional or unsupported claims across a long sustainability report is slow, and assurance must consider whether information is balanced and not misleading.
approach: Text-analysis models score tone, specificity and whether a claim is backed elsewhere in the report; flags tell the practitioner where to look.
Analyst commentary says KPMG uses NLP and machine learning to detect potential greenwashing in clients' reports; no result is given.
A university prototype on 150 DAX-company ESG reports found more specific wording went with stronger internal claim support (Spearman rho 0.310; independent).
The practitioner investigates each flag and decides whether more procedures are needed; the prototype aims to prioritise review, not classify greenwashing.

title: Idea: analytics over multi-year sustainability data and narrative-versus-number checks
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: unexplained changes, unit inconsistencies, restatements and narrative contradicting numbers are easy to miss when multi-year data arrives in many formats.
approach: Analytics or AI would scan reported data and narrative for unusual swings, missing values, inconsistent units and text contradicting the numbers.
For example, a sharp emissions fall might reflect a boundary or method change; no result is published.
The practitioner investigates each flag and decides whether it needs recalculation, source inspection, inquiry or control testing.

title: Idea: cross-check emissions and supplier claims against external data
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: much sustainability evidence comes from the entity or suppliers the practitioner cannot reach, leaving no independent source to compare reported claims against.
approach: AI tools would match reported figures with outside data: satellite images for site emissions, emission-factor databases, peer outliers, media and regulatory records.
Results would target procedures and corroborate evidence, not replace direct evidence.
The practitioner decides whether an external signal calls for further procedures at the entity or supplier; no result is published.

title: Idea: source-linked drafting of evidence matrices and workpaper summaries
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: sustainability engagements generate long reports, policies, datasets and correspondence that must be summarised and documented in the assurance file.
approach: Generative AI would summarise long documents, prepare a preliminary evidence matrix and draft descriptions of procedures.
Every output would be linked to its source, logged and reviewed by the team.
A reviewer corrects and source-checks all AI drafts before they enter the file; no result is published.

title: Idea: AI-supported risk assessment and planning priorities for sustainability engagements
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: ISSA 5000 asks for risk assessment across many topics, sites and value-chain components, and teams have limited time to allocate testing.
approach: AI would highlight high-risk areas, unusual metrics, missing evidence and inconsistent disclosures so the team can prioritise procedures and allocate resources.
The risk assessment itself remains the practitioner's; each AI signal is evaluated for relevance, materiality and need for more procedures.

title: Idea: continuous evaluation of digital sustainability data by automated tools
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: annual engagements review data months after the fact, so point-in-time sampling can miss problems in continuous meter or sensor feeds.
approach: Automated tools would run continuously over digital data, evaluate its relevance and reliability, and raise exceptions for the practitioner.
ISSA 5000 gives this as an example of how the practitioner may use automated tools.
The literature frames it as a move from retrospective document review to continuous, data-driven assurance.
The practitioner evaluates the relevance and reliability of the information and the tool's operation.

title: Reporting-team AI that checks disclosures against standards and drafts narrative
problem: Reporting teams compare long standards with existing content line by line, gaps that surface late can force new data under deadline, and they want drafts quickly but fear unsupported statements.
approach: Workiva's Sustainability Disclosure Agent marks each ESRS or ISSB requirement present, partial or missing in a scorecard and drafts a first version.
Workiva presents it as supporting expert judgement; the team keeps sign-off.
Preparers also use AI to draft narrative; vendors say it is valuable only if tied to verified data and human review.
No time, accuracy or usage figure is published; the team reviews the scorecard and draft before they enter the report.

title: Automated supplier data ingestion and spend-based Scope 3 classification with calculation lineage
problem: Scope 3 data arrives from hundreds of suppliers as PDFs, spreadsheets and inconsistent questionnaires, reconciling it takes weeks each cycle, and numbers without a traceable source are hard to verify.
approach: OCR extracts data from bills and supplier documents, agents standardise units and remove duplicates, and models map procurement lines to emissions categories.
Each output is meant to trace to its source, emission factor and approval history, which assurance providers need.
Vendor reports 90% less OCR data entry time and 65-80% less time to actionable data (vendor-published).
Vendor says Smiths Group completed its SB 261 report in two days (vendor-published); humans review outputs before use in disclosures.
who: Watershed, Smiths Group, Harris Farm Markets

title: AI gap-filling and estimates for missing or value-chain sustainability data (preparer side)
problem: Value-chain data is often unavailable or unreliable; reporting rules allow estimates, and the assurance provider must evaluate the data, methods and assumptions behind them.
approach: Tools flag data gaps and propose gap-fill methods such as proxy data, sector averages and estimation models, recording the assumption and rationale.
The vendor argues this record reduces friction with auditors; no result is published (vendor-published).
The practitioner considers assumptions, method changes and comparability, and whether assumptions fit external evidence and are free of management bias.

title: PwC Germany AI tool for clients' EU sustainability data and reports (CSRD)
problem: CSRD reporters must gather thousands of data points across the value chain and calculate many KPIs, and manual handling is slow and error-prone.
approach: PwC Germany's CSRD.AI Manager, built with SAP, extracts, organises and analyses data, calculates KPIs and speeds up report generation for clients.
It uses the firm's CSRD content and customisable data models, on SAP AI Core, HANA Cloud and Datasphere.
A PwC product owner says it removed a heavy resource drain for clients; no figure is given (self-reported).
The firm evaluates threats and safeguards before accepting a non-assurance service for an assurance client.

title: AI-assisted double materiality assessment by preparers, and assurance over that process
problem: The materiality assessment decides what is reported; it is large, judgement-heavy and a frequent source of assurance findings, and the practitioner must consider the entity's process to identify reportable information.
approach: Survey respondents name AI in materiality assessments a primary use case and an investment priority for the next three years (independent).
It was less popular than in the previous year's study, with some sign practitioners think the technology is not yet mature.
No time or quality figure is given.
The assurance provider must still understand and test the entity's process, whatever tool supports it.

title: Idea: assurance procedures over a client's AI-assisted sustainability reporting pipeline
problem: Idea only, not a deployment: as preparers draft and calculate with AI, the practitioner must obtain evidence about information from systems the team cannot easily inspect.
approach: Teams would extend their view of the client's information system to AI-assisted steps: tool, data, prompts, validation and route into the report.
A vendor suggests asking for traceability and a dry run of AI-generated reports with the auditor.
A sector site says assurance providers are developing methods for assessing AI-generated disclosures; no method is described.
The practitioner evaluates the reliability of information used as evidence, including whether its integrity was maintained through processing.
